rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abū al-Ḥasan analyzes the ellipsis gradually: يوم لا تجزي فيه loses فيه, yielding تجزيه, then loses the pronoun, yielding تجزي.
rows.anchor: اعتبر أبو الحسن في الحذف التدريج حيث أمكن

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh instead treats the preposition and pronoun as deleted together in one step.
rows.anchor: ومذهب سيبويه أنه حذف فيه دفعة واحدة

rows.speaker: أبو الفتح
rows.claim: Abū al-Fatḥ considers Abū al-Ḥasan’s stepwise deletion more convincing than deleting both elements at once.
rows.anchor: أبو الفتح 2 في المحتسب وقول أبي الحسن أوثق في النفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The usual analysis supplies a deleted clause, فضرب فانفجرت; the eruption itself signals the omitted striking, as with Moses striking the sea before it split.
rows.anchor: أنه معطوف على جملة محذوفة التقدير فضرب فانفجرت

rows.speaker: ابن عصفور
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṣfūr assigns the conjunction to the omitted ضرب and removes it from انفلق; al-Zarkashī calls this an outlandish contrivance.
rows.anchor: وابن عصفور يقول في مثل هذا إن حرف العطف المذكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqtitāʿ is retaining one letter of a word while dropping the rest; al-Zarkashī rejects the claim that this device never occurs in the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: الاقتطاع وهو ذكر حرف من الكلمة وإسقاط الباقي

rows.speaker: صاحب المثل السائر
rows.claim: The author of al-Mathal al-sāʾir denies that this kind of truncation occurs in the Qurʾān, a claim al-Zarkashī rejects.
rows.anchor: صاحب المثل السائر 1 ورود هذا النوع في القرآن العظيم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās treats the disconnected letters as abbreviations for divine names: alif-lām-mīm means أنا الله أعلم وأرى, and alif-lām-mīm-ṣād means أنا الله أعلم وأفصل.
rows.anchor: كما روى ابن عباس الم معناه أنا الله أعلم وأرى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some explain the bāʾ in برؤوسكم as the beginning of بعض, with the rest elided; the poem قفي لنا قالت قاف and the report كفى بالسيف شا illustrate similar truncation.
rows.anchor: إن الباء هنا أول كلمة بعض ثم حذف الباقي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the oath form من الله derives from أيمن, with its nūn deleted.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري في قوله من الله في القسم إنها ايمن التي تستعمل

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some recite يا مال by the form of tarḫīm that awaits completion; a salaf objected to such abbreviation in Hell, while others said its inhabitants were too distressed to finish the word.
rows.anchor: ولما سمعها بعض السلف قال ما أشغل أهل النار عن الترخيم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says no community asked fewer questions than Muḥammad’s community: its fourteen questions received answers, including this question and the listed questions in al-Baqara and other sūras.
rows.anchor: نقل عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أنه قال ما كان قوم اقل سؤالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The questions are arranged around two themes: asking about God’s essence and attribute in al-Baqara, then about the afterlife through questions about the mountains and the Hour.
rows.anchor: ولهذه المسألة ترتيب اثنان منها في شرح المبدأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two sūras beginning يا أيها الناس divide the themes similarly: al-Nisāʾ in the first half explains creation, while al-Ḥajj in the second treats the afterlife.
rows.anchor: انه ورد في القران سورتان اولهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first three questions appear without conjunction because they arose at separate times; the later questions are joined with wāw because they were asked together.
rows.anchor: لأن سؤالهم عن الحوادث الأول وقع متفرقا عن الحوادث

words: وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِى عَنِّى فَإِنِّى قَرِيبٌ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zarkashī raises why this answer begins directly with God’s nearness instead of the usual قل, as in the answer about the new moons; this excerpt leaves the question open.
rows.anchor: وعادة السؤال يجيء جوابه في القرآن بقل نحو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fragment says رأيت takes a direct object because it contains the sense of تنظر.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت من أين جاءت إلى ورأيت يتعدى بنفسه أجيب لتضمنه معنى تنظر

words: كما أخرجك ربك من بيتك بالحق
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Semantic connection can link clauses without a conjunction. The command about spoils is likened to the Prophet’s departure for Badr despite companions’ reluctance; they disputed the fighting and spoils, so the verse commands obedience.
rows.anchor: فإن الله سبحانه أمر رسوله أن يمضي لأمره في الغنائم

words: كما أخرجك ربك من بيتك بالحق
rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One reading attaches the comparison to المؤمنون حقا: they are true believers just as the Lord brought the Prophet out in truth, like the oath in 51:23.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه أولئك هم المؤمنون حقا كما أخرجك ربك من بيتك بالحق

words: كما أخرجك ربك من بيتك بالحق
rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another reading makes the kāf modify an omitted command: act over the spoils as you acted when leaving for Badr, despite the people’s dislike; compare the favor of sending a messenger in 2:151.
rows.anchor: وقيل الكاف صفة لفعل مضمر وتأويله افعل في الأنفال كما فعلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison in كما أنزلنا على المقتسمين requires an omitted object such as punishment: the Prophet is a clear warner of punishment like that sent on the dividers.
rows.anchor: فإن فيه محذوفا كأنه قال أنا النذير المبين عقوبة أو عذابا

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿAbbās distinguishes yāʾs omitted from the written text but retained in recitation from yāʾs omitted in both, then divides the first kind into pronoun and root-letter yāʾ.
rows.anchor: قال أبو العباس الياء الناقصة في الخط ضربان ضرب محذوف في الخط ثابت في التلاوة

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: The omitted yāʾ in فما آتاني marks Solomon’s knowledge and prophethood as an enduring, otherworldly gift that is better than the perishable worldly gifts given to the envoys.
rows.anchor: حذفت الياء لاعتبار ما آتاه الله من العلم والنبوة

words: فلا تسألن ما ليس لك به علم
rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: The omitted yāʾ in Noah’s prohibition concerns hidden, unseen knowledge; this differs from Moses’ question to al-Khiḍr about witnessed worldly events such as the boat, boy, and wall.
rows.anchor: غيب ملكوتى بدليل قوله

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: The written omission of the object pronoun in دعان signals a prayer arising from the unseen realm with inward sincerity.
rows.anchor: فحذف الضمير في الخط دلالة على الدعاء الذي من جهة الملكوت

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: ومن اتبعن means following God’s religion through bodily acts directed toward God and obedience.
rows.anchor: هو الاتباع العلمي في دين الله بالجوارح المقصود بها وجه الله

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: The yāʾ remains in مقامي because it concerns what is manifest to sight, while its omission in وعيد marks belief in an unseen warning conveyed through reports.
rows.anchor: ثبتت الياء في المقام لاعتبار المعنى من جهة الملك وحذفت من الوعيد

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Satan asks to have punishment postponed, not his body’s worldly life; this contrasts with the bodily delay requested in 63:10.
rows.anchor: ﴿ لئن أخرتن إلى يوم القيامة ﴾ هو التأخير بالمؤاخذة

words: عسى أن يهدين ربي لأقرب من هذا رشدا
rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: The guidance in the cave context is spiritual and enabled the Prophet to leave his people with his religion; Moses’ request for guidance to Midian concerns a perceptible route.
rows.anchor: سياق الكلام في أمور محسوسة والهداية فيه ملكوتية وقد هداه الله

words: على أن تعلمن مما علمت رشدا
rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: The request to learn right guidance belongs to the inward realm of guidance, continuing the passage’s distinction between hidden spiritual guidance and physical journeys.
rows.anchor: ﴿ على أن تعلمن مما علمت رشدا ﴾

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Moses’ prohibition ولا تتبعان concerns the path of guidance, not a physical journey to God; God had ordered him to deputize for and reform his people. Aaron’s فاتبعوني is physical following, since his command is concrete.
rows.anchor: هو فى طريق الهداية لا فى مسير موسى إلى ربه

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Wherever فكيف كان نكير occurs, the warning concerns the unseen realm: its visible effects have ended, while the enduring noun signals that God can similarly seize others.
rows.anchor: لأن النكير معتبر من جهة الملكوت لا من جهة أثره المحسوس

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Moses feared denial might stem from his own divinely inspired eloquence exceeding his audience’s comprehension and requiring an interpreter; their eventual denial would then be their own fault and complete the proof.
rows.anchor: خاف موسى عليه السلام أن يكذبوه فيما جاءهم به وأن يكون سببه من قبله

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: The wish expressed in إن كدت لتردين is an otherworldly, unseen intention.
rows.anchor: هو الإرادة الأخروي الملكوتي

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: The threat أن ترجمون refers to slander and false accusation, not being stoned.
rows.anchor: ليس هو الرجم بالحجارة إنما هو ما يرمونه من بهتانهم

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: فحق وعيد and the warning in لمن خاف مقامي وخاف وعيد are interpreted as otherworldly and belonging to the hidden realm.
rows.anchor: هو الأخروي الملكوتي

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: People wrongly infer their standing with God from worldly abundance or constricted provision; God tests both righteous and wicked to establish proof against creation.
rows.anchor: هذا الإنسان يعتبر منزلته عند الله في الملكوت بما يبتليه في الدنيا

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: When the omitted yāʾ is a word’s root ending, as in الداع, it signals a petitioner whose heart and ultimate aim are devoted to God in the unseen and afterlife rather than the present world.
rows.anchor: والقسم الثاني من الضرب الأول إذا كانت الياء لام الكلمة سواء كانت في الاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When people who pursue the world receive little, the answer is that God grants the immediate world only as much as He wills and to whom He wills.
rows.anchor: 5 فعلق ما يريد بالمشيئة والإرادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise to answer prayer, like ادعوني أستجب لكم, is qualified by God’s will, a qualification explained in the following discussion.
rows.anchor: ﴿ أجيب دعوة الداع إذا دعان ﴾ وقوله ﴿ ادعوني أستجب لكم ﴾ 7 فإنه معلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Usulists disagree whether applying an unrestricted text to a restricted one follows Arabic usage or analogy; proponents of the linguistic view cite Arabs’ preference for brevity and omission, as in عن اليمين وعن الشمال قعيد.
rows.anchor: اختلف الأصوليون في أن حمل المطلق على المقيد هل هو من وضع اللغة

rows.speaker: إمام الحرمين
rows.claim: Imām al-Ḥaramayn rejects the claim that the Qurʾān is like one verse, allowing unrestricted wording to be restricted elsewhere: only the eternal divine attribute is one, while its expressions are multiple and include opposites.
rows.anchor: قال إمام الحرمين وهذا غلط لأن الموصوف بالاتحاد الصفة القديمة المختصة بالذات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When unrestricted and restricted rulings concern the same subject, conflicting specifications—continuous fasting, broken fasting, or days left open—mean the original unrestricted wording remains unrestricted.
rows.anchor: والثاني كإطلاق صوم الأيام في كفارة اليمين وقيدت بالتتابع في كفارة الظهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Silence in a different ruling does not transfer a restriction: tayammum’s two limbs do not inherit ablution’s four, and a food option in one expiation cannot be imported into another.
rows.anchor: فأما إذا حكم في شيء بأمور لم يحكم في شيء آخر ينقض تلك الأمور

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some infer from the verse naming the day of the two armies’ encounter that it was the night of the seventeenth of Ramadan; the author notes that this dating is disputed.
rows.anchor: استنبط بعضهم هنا بيانا آخر وهو أنها ليلة سبعة عشر من قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of being humble toward believers and mighty against unbelievers is explained by the parallel wording in the conquest sūra.
rows.anchor: فسره في آية الفتح ﴿ أشداء على الكفار رحماء بينهم ﴾

words: يحلون فيها من أساور من ذهب
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of adornment and being guided to good speech is explained by the next sūra’s account of the saved praising God for removing grief.
rows.anchor: وقد فسره فى سورة فاطر

words: وإذا بشر أحدهم بما ضرب للرحمن مثلا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about being given the likeness assigned to the Merciful is clarified by the wording in al-Naḥl about being told of a daughter.
rows.anchor: بين ذلك بقوله فى النحل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān first mentions divorce in general terms, then explains it in Sūrat al-Ṭalāq.
rows.anchor: وذكر الله الطلاق مجملا وفسره في سورة الطلاق

words: إلا على أزواجهم أو ما ملكت أيمانهم
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception for spouses and those owned by the right hand is complemented by the other verse forbidding combinations such as two sisters, mother and daughter, and stepdaughter.
rows.anchor: فاستثنى الأزواج وملك اليمين ثم حظر تعالى الجمع بين الأختين

words: إن الله لا يهدي من هو كاذب كفار
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent claim that God guides no liar or ingrate is limited to those whom He knows are condemned; verses about the binding word explain why they will never believe.
rows.anchor: فإن ظاهره مشكل لأن الله سبحانه قد هدى كفارا كثيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Apparent nonresponse is qualified by the verse saying God uncovers what people call for if He wills; the Prophet explains that a sinless, non-estranging supplication is answered immediately, saved for the afterlife, or matched by averting harm.
rows.anchor: وكثير من الناس يدعون فلا يستجاب لهم وبيانه بقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: When a conditional clause introduced by wāw is circumstantial, it needs no apodosis: the clause functions like a dependent adverbial, normally a single constituent, rather than an independent sentence.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جني وإنما كان كذلك لأن الحال فضلة وأصل وضع الفضلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the conditional clause receives its own answer, the wāw is coordinative rather than circumstantial; otherwise the sentence would lack an apodosis.
rows.anchor: فإن أجيب الشرط كانت الواو عاطفة لا للحال نحو أحسن إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Condition and consequence normally differ in wording; where they appear identical, interpret an omitted wish or intention, as in whoever wishes to repent and when you intend to read the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: وقد يتحدان فيحتاج إلى التأويل كقوله

words: جزاؤه من وجد في رحله فهو جزاؤه
rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī parses جزاؤه as the subject and the conditional sentence as its predicate, with the visible noun replacing the pronoun: the original ending is فهو هو.
rows.anchor: فقال الزمخشري يجوز أن يكون جزاؤه مبتدأ والجملة الشرطية كما هي خبره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās resolves the apparent identity of condition and consequence by reading the clause as whoever God wills to guide is guided.
rows.anchor: قدره ابن عباس من يرد الله هدايته فلا يتحد الشرط والجزاء

words: وإن لم تفعل فما بلغت رسالته
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author notes this as another case where conditional and consequential wording may seem identical, adding that earlier interpretations of it were discussed elsewhere.
rows.anchor: ﴿ وإن لم تفعل فما بلغت رسالته ﴾ وقد سبق فيها أقوال كثيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A condition and consequence can also be close in meaning rather than identical, as in the statements about entering or being removed from the Fire and attaining success.
rows.anchor: كقوله تعالى ﴿ ربنا إنك من تدخل النار فقد أخزيته ﴾

rows.speaker: ابن مالك
rows.claim: Ibn Mālik objects to Ibn al-Ḥājib’s use of الرحمن as an example of a noun ending in added alif and nūn: it is a divine proper name, normally inseparable from the article and rarely bare except in vocative.
rows.anchor: أنكر ابن مالك على ابن الحاجب تمثيله ب الرحمن

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī, unaware of Ibn Mālik’s argument, dismissed it as stubbornness in disbelief; al-Shāṭibī’s line using رحمانا was criticized for intending the established divine name.
rows.anchor: ولم يحضر الزمخشري هذا الجواب فذكر أنه من تعنتهم في كفرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pattern فعيل often marks intensive or repeated active meaning—رحيم, سميع, قدير, and similar forms—rather than an object, as shown by قتيل and جريح, whose killing or wounding is not gradable.
rows.anchor: وأما فعيل فعند النحاة أنه من صيغ المبالغة والتكرار كرحيم وسميع وقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: فعيل can also function as a collective noun, as in رفيقا, ظهير, and نجيّا.
rows.anchor: وقد يجيء في معنى الجمع كقوله تعالى ﴿ وحسن أولئك رفيقا ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A problem is raised: negating the intensive نسيا does not logically negate any forgetfulness. The author points to the suitability of the phrase for the preceding verse endings and promises further answers.
rows.anchor: ومن المشكل ﴿ وما كان ربك نسيا ﴾ فإن النفي متوجه على الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same apparent problem arises with بظلام: negating an intensive form alone need not negate all injustice, though other verses explicitly deny every wrong, even an atom’s weight; twelve answers are cited elsewhere.
rows.anchor: وتقريره أنه لايلزم من نفي الظلم بصيغة المبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pattern فعّال also expresses intensive meanings, as in غفّار, منّان, توّاب, وهّاب, فعّال لما يريد, and صبّار شكور.
rows.anchor: وأما فعال فنحو غفار ومنان وتواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated warnings such as the question about the Day of Judgment, and قتل كيف قدر, may be emphatic repetition or two separate warnings; without conjunction, repetition more clearly signals emphasis and a single report.
rows.anchor: وكذا قوله ﴿ وما أدراك ما يوم الدين ثم ما أدراك ما يوم الدين ﴾

rows.speaker: بدر الدين بن مالك
rows.claim: Badr al-Dīn Ibn Mālik allows an emphatic sentence to be joined by a conjunction, not only by ثم, despite his father’s apparently narrower formulation.
rows.anchor: بدر الدين بن مالك في شرح الخلاصة 4 أن الجملة التأكيدية قد توصل بعاطف

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās, al-Zamakhsharī, Fakhr al-Dīn, and ʿIzz al-Dīn take the repeated command to fear God as emphasis on the same command, not as two different commands; this is semantic repetition, not verbal emphasis.
rows.anchor: كما قاله النحاس والزمخشري والإمام فخر الدين والشيخ عز الدين ورجحوا ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that the second اتقوا coordinates with ولتنظر is answered by the agreed parallel: وقولوا للناس حسنا coordinates with لا تعبدون إلا الله, not the intervening duty to parents.
rows.anchor: أجيب بأنهم قد اتفقوا على أن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated choice of Mary and repeated remembrance at the Sacred Monument could describe two separate acts; two acts of remembrance are more likely because the site calls for repeated remembrance.
rows.anchor: وهو الأقرب في الذكر لأنه محل طلب فيه تكرار الذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ paired request to glorify and remember God abundantly is another example of repeated wording.
rows.anchor: حكاية عن موسى ﴿ كي نسبحك كثيرا ونذكرك كثيرا ﴾ 4

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative أولئك is repeated in the description of those who disbelieve and in the description of the guided and successful.
rows.anchor: وقوله ﴿ أولئك الذين كفروا بربهم وأولئك الأغلال في أعناقهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An answer normally matches its question, but may redirect the hearer to the important issue, be broader to meet an overlooked need, or be narrower as circumstances require; al-Sakkākī calls redirection أسلوب الحكيم.
rows.anchor: الأصل في الجواب إن يكون مطابقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asked why the moon changes shape, people are told it marks times for people and pilgrimage, redirecting them from appearance to practical importance.
rows.anchor: لما قالوا ما بال الهلال يبدو رقيقا مثل الخيط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asked what to spend, people are told whom to support; the answer also says that whatever good they spend is the proper object of expenditure.
rows.anchor: سألوا عما ينفقون فأجيبوا ببيان المصرف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the elderly, wealthy ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ asked both what to spend and where to put it, so this occasion is not an example of an answer diverting from the question.
rows.anchor: نعم روى عن ابن عباس أنه قال جاء عمرو بن الجموح وهو شيخ كبير

rows.speaker: ابن القشيري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qushayrī says one question asked who should receive the expenditure and another asked its amount; the answer addresses each question directly.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن القشيري السؤال الأول كان سؤالا عن النفقة إلى من تصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s question to Moses about what is in his right hand matches the question and adds information.
rows.anchor: ونظيره ﴿ وما تلك بيمينك يا موسى ﴾ 3 فيكون طابق وزاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s question asks for God’s essence or genus, an invalid premise; Moses instead identifies God through attributes, then names Him Lord of Pharaoh and his ancestors to refute Pharaoh’s claimed lordship, finally challenging their intelligence.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك أجوبة موسى عليه السلام لفرعون حيث قال فرعون

rows.speaker: الشريف الرضي
rows.claim: One reported reading takes لم يكد يراها to mean that he saw the hand only with difficulty and delay because darkness was so dense.
rows.anchor: وحكى الشريف الرضي في كتاب الغرر ( 2 ) ثلاثة أقوال في قوله تعالى ﴿ لم يكد يراها ﴾ 3 الأول إنها دالة على الرؤية بعسر

rows.speaker: الشريف الرضي
rows.claim: A second reported view treats كاد as extra, making the phrase a pure denial that he saw it, since the layered darkness blocks sight.
rows.anchor: والثاني إنها زائدة والكلام على النفي المحض ونقله عن أكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: الشريف الرضي
rows.claim: A third reported view gives كاد the sense of intended, as in كدنا ليوسف: he did not intend to see it.
rows.anchor: والثالث إنها بمعنى أراد من قوله ﴿ كدنا ليوسف ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis supplies a test of vision when the hand is brought out; يراها is an adjective describing the darkness: layered darkness that he sees.
rows.anchor: وذكر غيره أن التقدير إذا أخرج يده ممتحنا لبصره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For أكاد أخفيها, one reading is that God intends to conceal the Hour for recompense, another treats كاد as extra, and a third ends the sentence at أكاد: I nearly bring it, then begins أخفيها.
rows.anchor: وقيل تم الكلام عند قوله ﴿ آتية أكاد ﴾ والمعنى أكاد آتي بها

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reads the verb with fatḥa, giving it the sense reveal; the ḍamma reading can mean conceal or reveal, while the fatḥa reading permits only reveal.
rows.anchor: وقرأ سعيد بن جبير ﴿ أكاد أخفيها ﴾ بفتح الألف أي أظهرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Concealing the Hour’s time strengthens people’s readiness because they fear its sudden arrival.
rows.anchor: ومعنى سترتها لأجل الجزاء لأنه إذا أخفى وقتها قويت الدواعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oil is only near to shining before fire touches it; نور على نور then states the actual light. The apparent problem is resolved by reading the wāw as circumstantial: it nearly shines while untouched, so it would shine once touched.
rows.anchor: فلم يثبت للزيت الضوء وإنما أثبت له المقاربة من الضوء
